title: How to Read a Cash Flow Statement as an Investor
summary: How to read a cash flow statement: what operating, investing and financing cash flows mean, which lines to check first, and why profit and cash can tell different stories.
body_markdown:
Not by itself. A cash outflow in the investing section can mean the company is buying equipment it needs to grow, and a financing outflow can mean it is repaying debt. Negative cash from operating activities deserves the closest look, because it means the core business used cash during the period, and that cash had to come from the balance sheet or from financing.


The SEC guide puts it plainly: no one financial statement tells the complete story. The[income statement](https://meetbenson.com/blog/how-to-read-an-income-statement/) shows whether the company made a profit, and the[balance sheet](https://meetbenson.com/blog/how-to-read-a-balance-sheet/) shows what it owns and owes at the end of the period. Read the three together, and compare a company with its own earlier filings and with competitors rather than with a rule of thumb.
